```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(haven)
library(ggplot2)
library(lmerTest)
```

## 1. Kernel smoothing

### Question 1

```{r}
data_grades <- read.csv("data_grades.csv")

# Some histograms first
bins <- c(20, 40, 80, 160)
results_hist <- data.frame()
for (b in bins) {
  h <- hist(data_grades$grade_Math, breaks=b, plot=FALSE)
  bin_width <- h$breaks[2] - h$breaks[1]
  results_hist <- rbind(results_hist, data.frame(
    x = h$mids,
    y = h$density,
    bins = b,
    width = bin_width
  ))
}

ggplot(results_hist, aes(x=x, y=y, width=width)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity") +
  facet_wrap(~bins, labeller=label_both)


# Do the kernels now
bandwidths <- c(0.05, 0.08, 0.1, 0.2)
kernels <- c("gaussian", "epanechnikov")

# Math
results <- data.frame()
for (bw in bandwidths) {
  for (kr in kernels) {
     d <- density(data_grades$grade_Math, bw=bw, kernel=kr)
     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      x = d$x,
      y = d$y,
      bw = bw,
      kernel = kr
    ))
  }
}

ggplot(results, aes(x=x, y=y, color=kernel)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~bw, labeller=label_both) +
  labs(x="Grade", y="Density", title="Math Grades")

# English
results <- data.frame()
for (bw in bandwidths) {
  for (kr in kernels) {
     d <- density(data_grades$grade_English, bw=bw, kernel=kr)
     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      x = d$x,
      y = d$y,
      bw = bw,
      kernel = kr
    ))
  }
}

ggplot(results, aes(x=x, y=y, color=kernel)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~bw, labeller=label_both) +
  labs(x="Grade", y="Density", title="English Grades")

```

### Question 2
The math grades have approximately "normal" distribution and the English grades a bit less so with a sharp peak at 4. The most obvious is the kernel play small role in comparison to the bandwidth. The bandwidth of 0.1 or 0.2 clearly shows the distribution and has very little noise.

### Question 3
```{r}

bandwidths <- c(0.25, 0.15, 0.1, 0.08)

# Create a function to avoid all the copy+paste
compute_density <- function(data, bandwidths, kernel="gaussian") {
  results <- data.frame()
  for (bw in bandwidths) {
    d <- density(data, bw=bw, kernel=kernel)
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      x = d$x,
      y = d$y,
      bw = bw,
      kernel = kernel,
      label = paste0(kernel, " bw=", bw)
    ))
  }
  return(results)
}

dens_support <- compute_density(data_grades$grade_Math[data_grades$HasSupport == TRUE], bandwidths)
dens_support$group <- "Support"

dens_no_support <- compute_density(data_grades$grade_Math[data_grades$HasSupport == FALSE], bandwidths)
dens_no_support$group <- "No Support"

results_q3 <- rbind(dens_support, dens_no_support)

ggplot(results_q3, aes(x=x, y=y, color=group, linetype=label)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_linetype_manual(values=c(
    "gaussian bw=0.25" = "longdash",
    "gaussian bw=0.15" = "solid", # best one
    "gaussian bw=0.1" = "dotted",
    "gaussian bw=0.08" = "dotted"
  )) +
  labs(x="Math grade", y="Density", 
       title="Math grade density by support group",
       color="Group", linetype="Bandwidth")

```

Here we use the Gaussian kernel (by default, but can be changed)

### Question 4

We can see that the supported students scored lower, but we can't conclude if the support increases the grade since the students were specifically selected because they were struggling.

## 2. Linear mixed models

```{r}
reg_lmm = lmerTest::lmer(grade_Math ~ HasSupport + (1|class), data = data_grades)
summary (reg_lmm)
```

### Question 1

The math support does help increase the grade, by an estimated 0.461 points. The uncertainty (Standard Error) is 0.042 and p < 0.001. The program does have a postivie effect.

### Question 2

```{r}
data_grades$grade_English_cent <- data_grades$grade_English - mean(data_grades$grade_English)

reg_Engl <- lmerTest::lmer(
  grade_Math ~ HasSupport * grade_English_cent + (1|class),
  data=data_grades, REML=FALSE)

summary(reg_Engl)
```
The interaction between the support and the English grade is statically significant with a estimate -0.128, SE 0.127 and p-value <2e-16. The negative value points that for students with higher English grade the support program is not effective.

### Question 3

```{r}
reg_Engl_rs = lmerTest::lmer(
  grade_Math ~ HasSupport * grade_English_cent + (grade_English_cent | class),
  data = data_grades,
  REML = FALSE )
summary(reg_Engl_rs)
```

Introducing random slopes in the model changes the conclusion and does not show significant interaction (p-value of 0.217) between the English grade the effectiveness of the support program.

### Question 4

```{r}
AIC(reg_Engl, reg_Engl_rs)
BIC(reg_Engl, reg_Engl_rs)
```
The random slopes model fits the data better according to both AIC and BIC. So the final conclusion is that there is no significant interaction between the English grade the effectiveness of the support program.
